title: Book 3 — Thalia, Chapter 109
paragraphs: In just the same way, if vipers and the winged serpents of the Arabians were produced in the ordinary course of their nature, man would not be able to live upon the earth. But as it is, when they couple, and the male is in the act of generation—when he lets go his seed—the female seizes his neck, and fastening on it does not relax her hold until she has eaten through it. The male then dies in the manner I have described, while the female pays the penalty for the male in this way: the young, while still in the womb, take vengeance for their father by eating through their mother, and having eaten through her belly they make their way out for themselves. Other serpents, which are not harmful to man, produce eggs and hatch from them a very large number of offspring. Vipers are distributed over all the earth; but the winged ones are found in great numbers only in Arabia and nowhere else. That is why they appear so numerous.
